title: The Love We Forgot
subtitle: A five-session study on friendship, loneliness, and the covenant of companions.
summary:
This study is for anyone who has more contacts than they have ever had and fewer friends than they can admit, and for the small groups willing to say so out loud. It walks slowly through five sessions on the love the modern world quietly demoted, on the loneliness that followed and the friendship C.S. Lewis said we stopped naming, on the covenant of David and Jonathan who bound their souls together in a court that wanted one of them dead, on the friend who wounds faithfully when a flatterer would have kept the peace, on the strange thing Jesus said the night before he died when he called his followers friends, and on the ordinary work of keeping a friendship alive in a mobile, distracted, exhausted age. It is built so a busy person or a volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it. Every silence has a backup. Every session ends in prayer rather than in the ache people already carried into the room.

This is not a study that stands above friendship and dispenses advice about it. The writer came to faith from atheism, was raised without a father, and knows the particular loneliness of the man who has learned to need no one. He does not point from a safe distance. He has been the friend who let the friendship starve because he was busy, who kept the acquaintance and lost the brother, who confused being surrounded with being known. He writes from inside the indictment. So will you. And the study will not pretend that friendship is a small thing you get to when the important loves are handled. Scripture calls friendship a love strong enough to knit two souls, faithful enough to wound, costly enough that the Son of God gave his life for his friends and then, astonishingly, called us that. We forgot it was a love at all. This study is the work of remembering.
audience: Anyone carrying loneliness, and the small groups that meet honestly

sessions.title: The Love We Stopped Naming
sessions.aim: To recover friendship as a real and serious love rather than a lesser bond you get to once the important relationships are handled, and to name the loneliness of the age not as a private failure but as the predictable fruit of a world that quietly demoted the very love it now aches for.
sessions.summary: A man told Bell, without drama, that if he were in the hospital he was not sure who he would call, and then added quickly that he was fine, that he had plenty of people. He was describing a life full of contacts and empty of friends, and he is not rare. He is the shape of the age. The real question is not why so many people are lonely but why we stopped treating friendship as a love worth building a life around, because C.S. Lewis wrote in 1960 that friendship is the least jealous of the loves and also the one the modern world most ignores, the one the ancients ranked highest and we barely rank at all. Aristotle had already sorted friendship into three kinds, the friendship of utility, kept because it is useful, the friendship of pleasure, kept because it is fun, and the friendship of virtue, the rare and slow bond of two people who want the good for each other and are made better by it, the only kind that lasts. Bell takes the strong case for the modern arrangement, that adults are busy, that family and work rightly come first, that friendship is a luxury for people with time. There is truth in it. But the arrangement is producing an epidemic, a loneliness the Surgeon General named a public health crisis in 2023, and a world of people optimizing everything except the one thing Scripture says it is not good to be, alone. Then the reversal. We did not lose friendship to bad luck. We traded it, for convenience, for mobility, for the thin company of a screen, and we are only now counting the cost. It is not good that the man should be alone. We built a world that forgot it, and then wondered why it aches.

keyScripture.why: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil, for if they fall, one will lift up his fellow, but woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up, naming companionship not as a luxury for the unhurried but as a basic human need, and solitude in the fall as a real danger and not a badge of strength.

discussion.q: Bell describes a man who had plenty of contacts and did not know who he would call from a hospital bed. Setting aside whether it is comfortable, is that closer to your life than you would like to admit, and how did it get that way?
discussion.behind: Open on the honest inventory before any theology. Most people have quietly accepted a life of acquaintance and would rather not name it. The point is not to shame anyone into a confession of loneliness but to let the gap between how connected we appear and how known we actually are come into the open. Land it on honesty, not on a fix. The naming is the first work.

discussion.q: Aristotle said most friendships are kept because they are useful or because they are fun, and only a few because two people actually want the good for each other. Look at your own friendships. Which kind are most of them, and does that surprise you?
discussion.behind: Give people a real tool and let them use it on themselves. Utility and pleasure friendships are not sins, they are normal and even good, but a life made entirely of them is thinner than it looks, because both dissolve the moment the usefulness or the fun runs out. Help the room notice how few friendships they have of the third kind, and let that noticing sit without rushing to repair it.

discussion.q: C.S. Lewis said friendship is the love the modern world most ignores, the one the ancients ranked highest and we barely rank at all. Why do you think we demoted it, and what did we tell ourselves we were gaining?
discussion.behind: Move from the personal to the cultural, gently. We did not decide to abandon friendship on purpose. We chose mobility, career, the nuclear household, the efficiency of the screen, each for a real good, and friendship was the quiet cost we did not see itemized. Help the room feel that the loneliness is not simply a personal failure but the fruit of a whole arrangement they were handed.

discussion.q: The Surgeon General called loneliness a public health crisis, as damaging to the body as smoking. Does it help or does it bother you to hear the ache named that plainly, and what does it tell you that a doctor had to say it before the church did?
discussion.behind: This is where the secular finding gets brought under Scripture. The research is real common grace, naming a genuine wound, and it is worth grieving that the culture measured the loneliness before the church addressed it. But keep the aim on Scripture, which said it first and said it deeper, that it is not good for the human to be alone. Let the finding confirm the diagnosis without becoming the whole of it.

discussion.q: Bell says we did not lose friendship to bad luck, we traded it, and he counts himself first among the traders. Where have you traded a friendship for something that seemed reasonable at the time, and what did you tell yourself?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication, and go first if the room is slow. The point is not to hunt for guilt but to see that the loneliness has a history each of us helped write, the unreturned call, the friend we let drift because we were busy, the community we skipped because we were tired. Grace means nothing until the trade is named as a trade. Confess your own before you ask for theirs.

objections.objection: I am not lonely, I am just an adult with responsibilities. Friendship is fine for people with free time, but between work and family there is nothing left over, and pretending everyone needs a circle of close friends is just romanticizing something optional.
objections.response: Grant what is honest in it, because there is real truth here. Adult life is full, the seasons of small children and demanding work are genuinely brutal on the calendar, and no one should be shamed for a thin stretch of years when survival takes everything. The demand to manufacture deep friendship on top of an already crushing load can itself be a cruelty. Grant all of that. Then name the gentler error. The objection assumes friendship is an extra, a hobby for the unhurried, when Scripture treats it as a need as basic as the one God named in the garden, that it is not good for the human to be alone. The busyness is real, but very often the busyness is also the alibi, the respectable name we give to a slow withdrawal from being known. The years without margin are real. So is the man who cannot say who he would call, and he did not get there by accident. He got there one reasonable postponement at a time.

objections.objection: I have plenty of friends. I talk to people all day, I have hundreds of connections online, and I never feel isolated. This whole loneliness panic is overblown, at least for people who put themselves out there.
objections.response: Take the confidence seriously rather than dismissing it, because being around people is real and social energy is a genuine gift. Some people are richly connected and should not be talked into a crisis they do not have. But press gently on the difference between company and friendship, because the two are easy to confuse and the age confuses them on purpose. To be surrounded is not the same as to be known. Aristotle's friendship of pleasure is real and good and also evaporates when the fun stops, and a feed full of connections is a marvel of contact that can leave a person entirely unknown. The test is not whether you feel isolated at a party. It is whether there is someone who could tell you the hard true thing, someone you would call in the worst hour, someone who has seen you at your least useful and stayed. If there is, thank God for it. If the honest answer is thinner than the number suggests, the crisis is not overblown, it is just well disguised.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Who is the friend you have let slowly slip into an acquaintance, and what is the reasonable-sounding excuse you have used to let it happen?
sessions.practice: This week, take one friendship you have allowed to thin into contact, and do the un-optimized thing. Do not text. Call, or better, show up, with no agenda and nothing to gain, the way a friend does who wants nothing but the person. Do not announce it as an experiment. And privately, make the honest list Bell describes, the people you would actually call from a hospital bed, and sit with what the length of it tells you. Write down what rises in you when you reach toward someone with no use in mind.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, in the garden you looked at a man who had everything and said it was not good for him to be alone, and we have built a world that forgot you said it. We are surrounded and unknown, full of contacts and short of friends, and we have called our loneliness busyness and our withdrawal maturity. Forgive the friendships we traded for convenience and never grieved. Teach us to want the good of another person more than we want their usefulness, to build the slow kind of love the ancients honored and we ignored. Give us the courage to reach toward someone with nothing to gain, and give us, in your mercy, the friend we would call in the worst hour, and make us that friend for someone else. Amen.
reflection: How much of my life is contact, and how little of it is friendship, and which have I been mistaking for the other?
Which of Aristotle's three friendships describes most of mine, and what would it cost me to build even one of the rare kind?
Where have I called my withdrawal from people maturity or busyness, when it was really a slow trading away of a love I now miss?
sessions.teaching: A man told Bell, without any drama in his voice, that he had recently wondered who he would actually call if he landed in the hospital, and had not been able to come up with a name he was sure of. Then he added, fast, the way people do, that he was fine, that he had plenty of people. Both things were true. He had plenty of people and not one he was sure of, a life full of contacts and empty of friends, and the reason his story matters is that he is not the exception. He is the shape of the age. So we begin not with a technique for making friends but with a harder question, which is why an entire civilization stopped treating friendship as a love worth building a life around, and only noticed once the loneliness had become a public emergency. C.S. Lewis saw it coming. In 1960, in The Four Loves, he wrote that friendship is in one sense the least natural of the loves, the least instinctive and biological, and precisely for that reason the one the modern world most ignores, where the ancient world ranked it near the top of human goods. The ancients were not sentimental about it. Aristotle, three centuries before Christ, had already done the careful work of sorting friendship into three kinds, and his sorting still cuts. There is the friendship of utility, the bond you keep because the other person is useful to you, the colleague, the contact, the person who can do something for you. There is the friendship of pleasure, the bond you keep because the other person is fun, the company that entertains, the good time. Both are real and neither is evil, but both share a fatal feature, they last exactly as long as the usefulness or the pleasure lasts and not one day longer, because you never loved the person, you loved what the person gave you. And then there is the third kind, the friendship of virtue, the slow and rare bond between two people who actually want the good for each other, who are made better by knowing each other, who would still be friends when the usefulness ran dry and the fun went quiet. That one lasts, Aristotle said, because it is built on the person and not on the transaction, and it is rare because it is slow, and we live in a world that has no patience for slow. Take the strong case for how we now live, because thoughtful people make it and it is not foolish. Adults are busy. Family rightly comes first, work is demanding, the seasons of raising children and building a career leave almost nothing over, and friendship, on this view, is a luxury for people with margin, something you get to later, if you get to it at all. Grant what is true, and much of it is. The busyness is not imaginary and the years without margin are brutal and real. But watch what the arrangement is producing, because the fruit is now impossible to ignore. In 2023 the Surgeon General of the United States issued a formal advisory naming loneliness and isolation an epidemic, a public health crisis, with effects on the body he compared to smoking. Let the strangeness of that land. It took a doctor to say what the garden said at the beginning, that it is not good for the human to be alone, and the church, which held that word the whole time, largely let the culture discover it first. Here is where I have to stand inside it, because I know this ground from the underside. I came to faith out of atheism, and I was raised without a father, and one of the first things you learn in that soil is how to need no one, how to be self-contained, how to call your isolation strength. I have let friendships die because I was busy and told myself they would keep. I have kept the acquaintance and lost the brother. I have been the man surrounded and unknown, and I dressed it up as independence. So when I say we did not lose friendship to bad luck, I mean I did not. I traded it, one reasonable postponement at a time, for convenience and mobility and the thin frictionless company of a screen that asks nothing and gives nothing back. That is the reversal this whole study turns on. The loneliness of the age is not a mystery and it is not merely a private failure. It is the bill coming due for a world that quietly decided the oldest human need was optional, and it is not good, God said before anything had gone wrong, for the human to be alone.

scriptureStudy.note: It is not good that the man should be alone. God names the one thing not good in a world he has been calling good, and he names it before the fall, before sin, in paradise. The need for another is not a weakness introduced by brokenness. It is written into what a human being is.

Two are better than one, for if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. The Preacher, who has tried everything and found most of it empty, lands on companionship as a plain good, and names the specific danger of the solitary life, that there is no one to lift you when you fall.

A threefold cord is not quickly broken. Companionship is not only comfort but strength, a structural thing, the difference between what snaps under strain alone and what holds because it is bound together. The isolated life is not merely sadder. It is weaker.

A man of many companions may come to ruin, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother. Scripture itself distinguishes the crowd of companions from the true friend, the many contacts from the one who stays, the exact distinction the age has lost.

Do not forsake your friend and your father's friend. Friendship in Scripture is meant to endure across time and even across generations, treated as a bond to be kept rather than a convenience to be dropped when a more useful arrangement appears.

The soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul. The Bible can speak of friendship in the language of souls knit together, a love so weighty it will occupy the whole of the next session, and nothing like a luxury for the unhurried.

No longer do I call you servants, but I have called you friends. The word friend is one Jesus reaches for at the most solemn moment of his life, which tells you what kind of love it is. If the Son of God ranks it this high, our demotion of it is not neutral.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the history the session only gestures at, because the West did not always rank friendship where we now do, and tracing the fall is worth the time. For the ancients, friendship was among the highest human goods, the subject of whole treatises, Aristotle devoting two books of the Nicomachean Ethics to it and Cicero writing his Laelius on Friendship near the end of his life as a kind of last testament. A group can weigh honestly what changed. The rise of the romantic ideal gradually made the marriage bond the one relationship expected to carry every human need, so that friendship, which the ancients had honored as its own love, came to look like a support role for the main event. The industrial and then digital reorganization of life scattered people across cities and screens, so that the ordinary proximity friendship needs, the neighbor, the parish, the guild, the long-settled place, simply dissolved. Set this beside Robert Putnam, whose study Bowling Alone traced the steep decline of American associational life across the second half of the twentieth century, the clubs and leagues and civic bodies that once wove people together thinning out year by year, and notice that the loneliness now measured as a health crisis has a documented social history and did not fall from the sky. Then take the harder turn under all of it. A culture that made the autonomous, self-choosing individual its highest value was always going to find friendship difficult, because friendship, real friendship of the third kind, binds you, obligates you, asks you to be inconvenienced by another person's life, and the sovereign self resists exactly that. The aim is not to despise the goods the modern world recovered, mobility and choice and freedom are real goods, but to see clearly the love those goods were quietly purchased with, and to ask whether the price was one anyone actually meant to pay.
sessions.caseStudy: A woman in your group is warm, capable, and well liked, the person everyone counts on, the organizer, the one who remembers birthdays and shows up with meals. When the conversation turns to being known rather than being useful, she goes quiet, and then says, almost as an aside, that she is not sure anyone knows her the way she knows them, that she is always the one giving and rarely the one seen. Here is the work for the leader, and it must honor her before it presses. Her giving is real and good and too rarely thanked, and you should say so plainly. But notice what she has just confessed under the competence, that she has built a life of being useful to people, Aristotle's friendship of utility run the generous direction, and it has left her surrounded and unknown, because a person who is only ever the helper is never actually a friend to anyone, only a resource. The danger is not that she gives too much. It is that the giving has become a way to be needed without the risk of being known, service as a hiding place. Do not let her reduce it to being underappreciated. Honor the giving fully, and still ask her, gently, whether she has any friend she lets carry her, or only friends she carries.

sessions.title: Souls Knit Together: The Covenant of David and Jonathan
sessions.aim: To see in David and Jonathan a friendship that rises to the level of covenant, sworn and costly and self-giving, and to recover the idea that friendship can be a bond you promise rather than a mood you enjoy, refusing both the sentimentality that makes it a feeling and the cynicism that makes it a transaction.
sessions.summary: Bell says the most radical friendship in Scripture is not radical because of its warmth but because of its cost, because Jonathan was the crown prince of Israel and David was the man God had chosen to take his throne, and Jonathan loved him anyway. The soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, the text says, and then it does something we rarely do with friendship. It calls the bond a covenant. Jonathan made a covenant with David because he loved him as his own soul, and then he took off his own robe and gave it to David, the robe of the heir, handing over the very future the friendship should have made him fight for. The real question is what kind of love that is, because it is not the friendship of utility, David could do nothing for Jonathan but cost him a throne, and it is not the friendship of pleasure, it was forged in a court where Jonathan's own father was hunting David to kill him. It is the third kind and past it, a friendship that became a covenant, sealed with an oath in the name of the Lord, that outlived Jonathan himself. Bell takes the strong case for keeping friendship light, that promises belong to marriage and blood, that friendship is precious precisely because it is free and unbound and you can walk away. There is something true in it. But David and Jonathan show a friendship that chose to bind itself, and the binding is exactly what let it hold when Saul's spears and the politics of succession would have shattered anything looser. Then the turn. When Jonathan died, David sang that his love had been extraordinary, surpassing the love of women, and the church has spent centuries embarrassed by the line, trying to make it something other than what it is, a man grieving the friend who loved him enough to give up a kingdom. We have no category for that anymore. Scripture did.

keyScripture.why: Then Jonathan made a covenant with David, because he loved him as his own soul, naming friendship in the language of covenant, a bond sworn and sealed rather than merely felt, and showing that the deepest friendship in Scripture was one that chose to bind itself by promise.

discussion.q: Jonathan was the heir to the throne, and David was the one chosen to take it, and Jonathan loved him anyway and even helped him. What is astonishing to you about a friendship where one person actively gives up his own future for the other?
discussion.behind: Open on the sheer cost, before any theology. Most friendships never test whether they would survive the friend's advantage over us. Jonathan's did, and he chose David over his own crown. Help the room feel how rare and even unnatural that is, a love that wants the friend's good more than its own throne, and let the strangeness of it sit before it is explained.

discussion.q: The text says Jonathan's soul was knit to David's, and then it calls their bond a covenant, sworn in the name of the Lord. What changes when you think of a friendship as something you could promise rather than only something you feel?
discussion.behind: Press on the category shift. We reserve promises for marriage and blood and treat friendship as a mood that lasts while it lasts. Scripture puts a friendship under oath. Help the room consider whether the lightness we prize in friendship is also what makes it so easy to let die, and what it might mean to actually commit to a friend, not romantically, but faithfully.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case that friendship is precious precisely because it is free, unbound, something you can walk away from, unlike marriage or family. What is true in that, and what does the freedom cost us?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. There is real good in the freedom of friendship, its lack of legal entanglement, its being chosen rather than assigned. But the same lack of binding is why friendship is the first thing to go when life gets busy, the relationship with no vow to hold it. Help the room feel the trade, that the very freedom we cherish is also the reason so many friendships quietly dissolve.

discussion.q: When Saul was hunting David, Jonathan went to him in the wilderness and, the text says, strengthened his hand in God. What does it look like for a friend to strengthen your hand in God rather than just cheer you up, and who has done that for you?
discussion.behind: Move to the concrete and the spiritual center. Jonathan did not merely comfort David, he pointed him back to God in the worst hour. This is the friendship of virtue at its height, the friend who wants your good all the way down to your soul. Help the room name the difference between a friend who distracts you from the pit and one who meets you in it and points you up.

discussion.q: David grieved that Jonathan's love was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women, and the church has often been embarrassed by that line. Bell says we have simply lost the category. Have we lost the ability to love a friend that deeply, and what did we lose it to?
discussion.behind: Close on the loss and the self-implication. The discomfort with David's grief says more about us than about him, revealing a culture that can only read deep love as romance and has no room for a friendship worth weeping over. Help the room mourn the category we misplaced, and go first by naming a friendship you let go thin that could have been this, had you let it.

objections.objection: The whole David and Jonathan story is being read too intensely. They were allies in a dangerous political situation, and calling it a covenant of the soul is projecting modern ideas of deep friendship onto what was really a strategic alliance.
objections.response: Grant the caution, because reading our longings into an ancient text is a real danger and the political situation was genuinely dangerous and real. Jonathan and David were caught in a lethal succession crisis, and that context matters and should not be flattened. But the text will not let the bond be reduced to strategy, because a strategic alliance runs on utility, and everything Jonathan does runs against his own utility. An heir does not strengthen the hand of the man who will take his throne, does not warn him against his own father, does not hand over his royal robe, unless something other than advantage is at work. Scripture names that something plainly and repeatedly, a soul knit to a soul, a covenant sworn before God, a love Jonathan chose at the direct cost of his crown. You do not have to romanticize it to take it seriously. You only have to read what it says and notice that no calculation of interest explains a single thing Jonathan did.

objections.objection: Making friendship into a covenant sounds suffocating. The beauty of friendship is that it is free, with no obligations and no strings, and turning it into a sworn commitment would just make it another duty like everything else in life.
objections.response: Hear the real fear, because it is pointing at something worth protecting. Friendship should not become one more contractual burden, and a version of this that turns friends into obligations to be managed would drain the very freedom that makes friendship a gift. Grant that fully. But notice what the covenant in the story actually does, because it does not suffocate the friendship, it saves it. It is precisely because Jonathan and David are bound by oath that the friendship survives Saul's spears, the years of exile, the politics that should have made them enemies. The bond with no strings is also the bond with nothing to hold it when strain comes, which is why so many of our unbound friendships quietly evaporate under nothing more dramatic than busyness. Covenant here is not a cage. It is the thing that lets a friendship weather what would otherwise end it, a chosen faithfulness that says I will not let this drift, rather than a legal chain that says you cannot leave.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Is there a single friend you would give up an advantage for, the way Jonathan gave up a throne, and if the honest answer is no, what does that tell you about how you have loved your friends?
sessions.practice: This week, do one Jonathan thing, one act of friendship that costs you something and gains you nothing, that puts a friend's good above your own advantage in a place where the two actually compete. And find one friend and, without making it strange, tell them plainly that you are committed to them, that you are not going to let the friendship drift, the closest thing to Jonathan's covenant you can honestly offer. Write down what it stirs in you to love a friend at a cost, and whether you have been keeping your friendships too light to ever be tested.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you gave David a friend who loved him enough to give up a throne, who knit his soul to another and sealed it with an oath in your name, and who went to him in the wilderness and strengthened his hand in you. We have loved our friends more lightly than that, kept them unbound so we could keep them convenient, and let the deep ones drift for want of a promise. Forgive the friendships we held too loosely to ever be tested. Teach us to want a friend's good above our own advantage, to bind ourselves in faithfulness where we have only ever felt fondness, to strengthen a friend's hand in you rather than merely cheer them up. And give us, and make us, the friend who stays when the spears fly. Amen.
reflection: Have I ever loved a friend at real cost to myself, or have I kept my friendships in the range where they never ask anything of me?
What would it mean to make a covenant of faithfulness with a friend, not a romance and not a contract, but a promise not to let it drift?
Who has strengthened my hand in God in a hard season, and whose hand am I strengthening now, or have I only offered distraction where a friend was needed?
sessions.teaching: Bell says the most radical friendship in the Bible is not radical because of how warm it was but because of how much it cost, and to feel the cost you have to hold the whole situation in view. Jonathan was the crown prince of Israel, the son of King Saul, the natural heir to the throne. David was the shepherd God had secretly chosen to take that throne instead, the man whose very existence was a threat to everything Jonathan stood to inherit. Every rule of self-interest said they should be rivals, and Jonathan's own father understood the situation perfectly and spent years trying to put a spear through David's chest to protect his son's succession. And into that, the text drops a sentence that should stop us. The soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and he loved him as his own soul. Then it does the thing we almost never do with friendship. It reaches for the language of covenant. Jonathan made a covenant with David, because he loved him as his own soul, and to seal it he took off his own robe and gave it to David, along with his armor, his sword, his bow, his belt. Read that slowly, because it is not a sentimental gesture. The robe of the heir is the sign of the throne, and Jonathan hands it to the very man who will sit on that throne in his place. He is not just giving a gift. He is handing over his future, blessing the friend who costs him everything. So we have to ask what kind of love this is, and the categories from the first session make the answer sharp. It is not the friendship of utility, because David can do nothing for Jonathan except take his crown. It is not the friendship of pleasure, because it is forged in a court where the friend's father is hunting the friend to kill him, which is nobody's idea of a good time. It is the third kind, the friendship of virtue, the love that wants the good of the other person, and it has risen past even that into covenant, a bond sworn in the name of the Lord and sealed with an oath. Take the strong case for keeping friendship lighter than this, because thoughtful people make it. Promises, the argument runs, belong to marriage and to blood. The glory of friendship is precisely that it is free, unbound, chosen fresh each day and not required, and you can always walk away, and that freedom is what makes it a gift rather than a duty. There is something true in that, and I do not want to lose it. Friendship is chosen, and the choosing is part of the beauty. But watch what the covenant actually does in the story, because it does not cage the friendship, it saves it. It is exactly because Jonathan and David are bound by oath that the bond survives what would shatter anything looser, the spears, the years of David's exile, the whole crushing logic of succession that should have made them enemies. When David is at his lowest, hunted in the wilderness of Ziph, the text says Jonathan rose and went to him and strengthened his hand in God. Sit with that phrase, because it is the friendship of virtue at its very summit. Jonathan did not send encouragement from a safe distance. He crossed into the wilderness where the hunted man was hiding, at risk to his own life, and he did not merely comfort David, he strengthened his hand in God, pointed him back to the One who had promised him the throne, refused to let his friend despair. Here is where I have to be honest about myself, because I have loved my friends more lightly than Jonathan loved David, and I know why. Loving lightly is safe. A friendship you keep unbound is a friendship that can never really cost you, never really test you, never ask you to cross into anyone's wilderness. I have kept my friendships in the range where they ask nothing, and called it respecting their freedom, when often it was protecting my own. And then the ending, which the church has never quite known what to do with. When Jonathan was killed in battle, David sang a lament, and in it he said that Jonathan's love to him had been extraordinary, surpassing the love of women. For centuries readers have squirmed at that line, worked hard to make it mean something other than what it says, because we have exactly one category for a love that deep and it is romance, and so we assume the verse must be about that or must be exaggeration. But the simpler and harder truth is that we have lost the category Scripture assumed, the category of a friendship worth weeping over, a companion love so weighty a king would mourn it in the language of the greatest loves he knew. David was not confused about what kind of love it was. We are. He grieved a friend who had loved him enough to give up a kingdom, and he had a word for it, and the word was friendship, and we have made that word so small that his grief no longer fits inside it.

scriptureStudy.note: The soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul. Scripture describes friendship in the language of souls bound together and of loving another as oneself, a weight of love we now reserve for romance, applied here to a friend.

Jonathan made a covenant with David, and he gave David his robe and his armor. The heir hands the sign of the throne to the man who will take it. The covenant is sealed not with words only but with the surrender of Jonathan's own future to his friend's good.

Jonathan warned David, though his father Saul sought to kill him. Friendship here means siding with the friend even against one's own father and one's own dynastic interest, choosing the covenant of the soul over the bond of blood and the pull of the throne.

Jonathan made David swear again by his love for him, for he loved him as he loved his own soul. The covenant is renewed and extended to descendants, a friendship deliberately built to outlast the two friends themselves, bound across generations like the marriage covenant.

Jonathan rose and went to David at Horesh, and strengthened his hand in God. The truest office of a friend is not to distract from the pit but to enter it and point the friend back to God. Jonathan risks his life to do for David's soul what David cannot do alone.

Go in peace, because we have sworn both of us in the name of the Lord. Their parting is grounded in an oath before God, which makes their friendship a three-party bond, the two of them and the Lord who witnessed it, exactly as marriage is described elsewhere.

I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan; very pleasant have you been to me; your love to me was extraordinary. David grieves a friend in the language of the deepest loves he knows, and the church's long embarrassment at the line exposes how small our idea of friendship has become.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the way the Christian tradition once thought about deep friendship, because the church has resources here it has largely forgotten. In the twelfth century Aelred of Rievaulx, a Cistercian abbot, wrote a whole treatise called Spiritual Friendship, taking up Cicero's earlier work on the subject and baptizing it, arguing that friendship of the truest kind is not a distraction from the love of God but a school for it, and even daring the phrase that God is friendship, drawing on the claim that God is love. A group can weigh this carefully. Aelred took the friendship of virtue that Aristotle described and set it inside the life of the church, treating a deep friend as a gift through whom one learns to love God more truly, which is a far higher account of friendship than our culture's, and arguably higher than much of the modern church's. Set this beside the caution the tradition also carried, that friendship can become exclusive, a closed circle of two that shuts others out or that loves the friend more than God, and notice that the tradition held both, the exalted good of deep friendship and the real danger of making an idol of it. Then take the harder turn back to David and Jonathan and the discomfort their story provokes. The modern reader's instinct to sexualize any intense same-sex love, or else to flatten it into mere alliance, reveals a culture that has genuinely lost the middle category the ancients and the medievals kept, a love between friends that is neither romance nor transaction but its own real and honorable thing. A group should ask what was lost when that category collapsed, and whether the recovery of covenant friendship, deliberate, faithful, spiritually serious, and chaste, is one of the gifts the church could offer a lonely age. The aim is to reach back past our thinned-out idea of friendship to a tradition that took it seriously enough to write treatises on it, and to ask what it would cost us to take it that seriously again.
sessions.caseStudy: A man in your group speaks warmly about his friends but, when the covenant theme comes up, grows a little defensive and says he does not really do the deep, intense thing, that he keeps his friendships easy and low-maintenance and that suits him fine. He is not cold, and he clearly has people he likes and does things with. Here is the work for the leader, and it must honor him before it presses. Easy and low-maintenance friendships are real and good, and a man is not obligated to turn every friendship into a covenant of the soul, so do not treat his preference as a defect to be corrected. But notice what low-maintenance can quietly mean, that he has arranged his friendships so none of them can ever cost him anything or ask anything of him, Aristotle's friendships of pleasure kept deliberately in the shallows. The danger is not that his friendships are light. It is that he may have made sure they stay light so that he never has to be the friend who crosses into a wilderness, never has to be known past the easy surface, never has to risk what Jonathan risked. Do not shame the preference for ease. Honor it, and still ask him, gently, whether there is a single friend he would let his life be inconvenienced for, or whether low-maintenance has become the name he gives to keeping everyone at a safe and manageable distance.

sessions.title: Faithful Are the Wounds of a Friend
sessions.aim: To recover the friend who tells the hard truth as an act of love rather than a breach of it, to see honesty and accountability as offices of true friendship, and to refuse both the false peace that calls flattery kindness and the harshness that calls cruelty honesty.
sessions.summary: Bell says the surest sign you do not actually have a close friend is that no one has told you a hard truth about yourself in years, because a friend is not mainly someone who makes you feel good, a friend is someone who tells you the thing that is true. Proverbs says it with a bluntness we have lost the stomach for, that faithful are the wounds of a friend but profuse are the kisses of an enemy, which turns our instincts upside down, because we treat the person who only affirms us as the good friend and the person who challenges us as the difficult one, when Scripture says the flatterer is the enemy and the one who wounds you is the faithful one. The real question is why we have built friendships that cannot survive an honest word, and the answer is that we have confused friendship with agreement and love with approval. Iron sharpens iron, Proverbs says, and one man sharpens another, but iron sharpening iron is not a gentle process, it throws sparks, it grinds, it wears down what needs to come off. Bell takes the strong case for gentleness, that the world is already full of critics, that people are fragile and wounded and need encouragement more than correction, that the church especially has a long ugly record of cruelty dressed up as truth-telling. He grants every bit of it, and grants that much harm has been done by people who called their contempt honesty. But the honesty that wounds faithfully is not the same as the harshness that wounds carelessly. The difference is whether the wound is for the friend's good or for the speaker's satisfaction. Then the reversal and the self-implication. The reason we do not tell our friends the hard truth is rarely that we are protecting them. It is that we are protecting ourselves, the comfort of the friendship, our own standing, the risk of the hard conversation. We call our silence kindness. It is usually just cowardice wearing kindness as a coat.

keyScripture.why: Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy, naming the hard truth spoken in love as an act of faithfulness and the endless flattery of the one who will not risk honesty as a form of enmity, overturning our instinct that the friend is the one who only ever affirms us.

discussion.q: Bell says the surest sign you have no close friend is that no one has told you a hard truth about yourself in years. By that measure, do you have a close friend, and when did someone last love you enough to wound you?
discussion.behind: Open with the uncomfortable test, gently. Most people have never thought to measure friendship this way, and the honest answer is often unsettling, that no one has risked a hard word in a long time. The point is not to make anyone feel unloved but to expose how our friendships have quietly been arranged around comfort. Let the silence after the question do its work.

discussion.q: Proverbs calls the friend who wounds faithful and the one who only flatters an enemy. Why does that reverse our instincts, and where have you treated the challenging friend as the difficult one and the flatterer as the good one?
discussion.behind: Press on the inversion. We instinctively reward the friend who affirms us and quietly resent the one who challenges us, exactly backwards from Proverbs. Help the room notice whom they have pulled closer and whom they have pushed away, and whether comfort rather than truth has been the real basis of their choosing. Keep it self-directed, not a license to go correct people.

discussion.q: Iron sharpens iron, Scripture says, and the process throws sparks and grinds. What does it actually feel like to be sharpened by a friend, and are you in any friendship close enough for that grinding to happen?
discussion.behind: Move to the concrete image. Sharpening is not gentle, it involves friction and resistance and the wearing away of what should not be there. Help the room feel that a friendship with no friction at all is not necessarily healthy, it may just be too shallow to sharpen anything. Ask whether they have any friendship close enough to produce sparks, and whether they have avoided that closeness on purpose.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case that people are fragile and need encouragement more than correction, and that the church has done real harm with cruelty dressed as honesty. What is true in that, and where is the line between wounding faithfully and just wounding?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves carefully. The caution is real, the world is full of critics and the church has a genuine record of cruelty in truth's name, and no one should leave this session licensed to go be harsh. But the line is real too, and it runs through motive, whether the hard word is for the friend's good or for the speaker's own satisfaction. Help the room locate the line without either weaponizing honesty or abandoning it.

discussion.q: Bell says the real reason we stay silent with our friends is not to protect them but to protect ourselves, and calls it cowardice wearing kindness as a coat. Where have you called your silence kindness when it was really self-protection?
discussion.behind: Close on the self-implication, and go first. We tell ourselves we withhold the hard truth to spare the friend, but usually we are sparing ourselves the risk and the discomfort. Help the room see that the loving thing and the hard thing are often the same thing, and that the silence we congratulate ourselves for is frequently a failure of love, not an expression of it. Name your own withheld word before asking for theirs.

objections.objection: Constantly correcting your friends is exhausting and arrogant. Who made you the judge of everyone? People need friends who accept them as they are, not friends who are always pointing out their faults and calling it love.
objections.response: Grant what is right in the anger, because it is aimed at something real. There are people who mistake a critical spirit for honesty, who correct constantly not out of love but out of a need to feel superior, and being around them is exhausting and often wounding in the careless way, and Scripture has no more patience for that than you do. Acceptance is a real gift of friendship and the friend who receives you as you are is not doing something small. Grant all of it. Where the objection overshoots is in throwing out faithful wounding along with careless wounding, as if the only options were constant criticism or unconditional approval. Proverbs knows a third thing, the rare, costly, well-timed hard truth spoken by someone who has earned the right through years of love, not the reflexive fault-finding of the critic but the reluctant honesty of the friend who would rather not say it and says it anyway because your good requires it. The test is frequency and motive. The critic wounds often and enjoys it. The friend wounds rarely and hates it, and does it only because a flatterer would be an enemy.

objections.objection: If a friend really cared about me, they would support me, not judge my choices. Telling me hard truths I did not ask for is just imposing your opinion on my life, and I get to decide what is right for me.
objections.response: Hear the fairness in it, because there is a real boundary here worth honoring. No one is owed unsolicited commentary on every decision, friends are not appointed managers of each other's lives, and a person does get to make their own choices and live with them. Grant that. But notice the assumption underneath, that support and honesty are opposites, that to love someone is to affirm whatever they decide, and Scripture will not allow that equation. The friend who watches you walk toward something destructive and says nothing, calling it respect for your autonomy, is doing to you exactly what Proverbs calls the enemy's kiss, the pleasant silence that costs the speaker nothing and costs you everything. Real support sometimes looks like the hard word you did not want, spoken by someone with no motive but your good. You do get to decide what is right for you. A true friend also gets to love you enough to tell you when they fear you are wrong, and then to keep loving you whichever way you choose. The autonomy is real. So is the friend who would betray you by staying silent.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the hard true thing a good friend would tell you right now if they loved you enough to risk it, and why has no one said it, or why have you arranged your life so no one could?
sessions.practice: This week, do the harder of the two things. Either receive a hard truth, by going to a trusted friend and asking them, genuinely, to tell you a blind spot they have seen and been too kind to name, and then not defending yourself when they do. Or speak one, by going to a friend you have watched walk toward something costly and saying the true thing you have been swallowing, gently, for their good and not your satisfaction. Write down what you were afraid of, and whether the fear was really for them or really for you.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you gave us a proverb we do not have the stomach for, that the wounds of a friend are faithful and the kisses of an enemy are many, and we have built friendships that cannot survive a single honest word. We have called the flatterer a good friend and the truth-teller difficult, and we have kept silent where love required speech and named our cowardice kindness. Forgive the hard words we swallowed to protect ourselves and dressed up as protecting others. Give us friends who love us enough to wound us, and make us those friends, willing to throw sparks for another's good, reluctant and honest and never cruel. Teach us the difference between the harshness that serves the speaker and the wound that serves the friend. And let us be sharpened, even where it grinds. Amen.
reflection: When did a friend last tell me a hard truth, and if it has been a long time, have I made myself un-tellable?
Whom have I pulled close because they affirm me, and whom have I quietly pushed away because they challenge me?
Where have I stayed silent with a friend and called it kindness, when it was really cowardice protecting my own comfort?
sessions.teaching: Bell says the surest single sign that you do not actually have a close friend is not that you feel lonely at parties. It is that no one has told you a hard truth about yourself in years. Sit with how strange that is as a diagnosis, because it runs against everything the culture trains us to want from friendship. We want friends who make us feel good, who take our side, who tell us we are right, and by that standard the best friend is the one who affirms us most reliably. Scripture says something almost the reverse. A friend, in the biblical account, is not mainly someone who makes you feel good. A friend is someone who tells you the thing that is true, especially when it is the thing you least want to hear, and the proverb that carries this says it with a bluntness we have lost the stomach for. Faithful are the wounds of a friend, but profuse are the kisses of an enemy. Read it slowly, because it inverts our whole instinct. The one who wounds you, when the wound is faithful, is the friend. The one who covers you in agreement and approval and never risks a hard word, whose kisses are profuse, is functioning as the enemy, because the flattery costs the flatterer nothing and leaves you unchanged and unwarned. We have this exactly backwards. We treat the person who only ever affirms us as the good friend and the person who challenges us as the difficult one we are patient with, when Proverbs would call the first one an enemy in disguise and the second one the rare real thing. So the question is why we have built friendships that cannot survive an honest word, and the answer is that somewhere we quietly confused friendship with agreement, and love with approval, until a friend became someone whose job is to validate us. But Scripture has a different picture, and it is not a gentle one. Iron sharpens iron, Proverbs says, and one man sharpens another. That image is worth staying with, because sharpening is not a soft process. When iron sharpens iron there is friction, there are sparks, there is the grinding away of the dull and the bent and the chipped, metal against metal until an edge appears. A friendship that produces no friction at all may not be a peaceful friendship. It may just be too shallow to sharpen anything, two blades that never touch. Take the strong case for gentleness, because it is a real case and I hold much of it myself. The world is already overstuffed with critics. People are more fragile and more wounded than they let on, carrying hurts you cannot see, and most of them need encouragement far more than they need one more person pointing out their faults. And the church, God help us, has a long and ugly record here, a history of cruelty dressed up as truth-telling, of people who used the language of honesty to license their contempt, who wounded carelessly and called it love and left real damage behind. Grant all of it, without hedging, because it is true and it matters. But watch the move the objection makes, because it throws out the faithful wound along with the careless one, as if the only choice were constant harsh correction or endless soft approval. Proverbs knows a third thing. The faithful wound is not the critic's reflex. It is rare, it is costly, it is well-timed, and it comes from someone who has earned the right through years of proven love, someone who would genuinely rather not say the hard thing and says it anyway because your good requires it. The difference between wounding faithfully and just wounding runs straight through motive. Is the hard word for the friend's good, or for the speaker's satisfaction. Does the person wound reluctantly and rarely, hating the necessity, or wound often and enjoy it. That line is real, and it is not hard to feel from the inside which side of it you are on. And now the reversal, which is the part I know from the inside and do not enjoy admitting. The real reason we do not tell our friends the hard truth is almost never that we are protecting them. We tell ourselves it is, we say we do not want to hurt them, we say it is not our place, we say they are going through enough. But underneath, most of the time, we are protecting ourselves, the comfort of the friendship, our own standing in their eyes, the sheer discomfort and risk of the hard conversation. I have watched friends walk toward things I feared would cost them, and I have said nothing, and I have called my silence kindness, and it was not kindness. It was cowardice wearing kindness as a coat. The loving thing and the hard thing are so often the same thing, and the gap between them is filled by our own fear. A friend who will risk the wound loves you more than a friend who will only risk the kiss, and if you want to know whether you have friends of the first kind, ask when one of them last told you something true that hurt. And if you want to know whether you are a friend of the first kind, ask whom you have been sparing, and whether you were really sparing them, or sparing yourself.

scriptureStudy.note: Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy. The verse inverts our instincts, naming the honest wound as faithfulness and the endless flattery as enmity, and forcing us to ask whether the friends we have chosen are chosen for their truth or only for their comfort.

Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another. Sharpening requires friction and produces sparks. A friendship with no edge and no resistance may simply be too shallow to sharpen anyone, two blades kept carefully from ever touching.

Better is open rebuke than hidden love. Love that stays hidden, that feels affection but never risks the hard word, is worth less, Scripture says, than an honest rebuke. The friend who will not speak is loving in a way that helps no one.

Oil and perfume make the heart glad, and the sweetness of a friend comes from his earnest counsel. The sweetness of a true friend is located not in agreement but in earnest counsel, the willingness to think hard about your good and tell you what he sees.

Whoever rebukes a man will afterward find more favor than he who flatters with his tongue. The hard word, though it stings first, earns deeper trust in the end, while the flatterer's easy approval, pleasant now, is finally worth nothing and known to be worth nothing.

If anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness. The New Testament pairs honesty with gentleness, ruling out both the silence that abandons a friend to his sin and the harshness that wounds him carelessly while correcting him.

Speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in every way into him. Truth and love are held together, not traded off. The goal is not truth that wounds for its own sake nor love that flatters into decay, but the honest word whose whole aim is that the friend grow.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the way honesty and accountability actually work in friendship, testing what the culture says against what Scripture says. The modern therapeutic account of relationships tends to prize affirmation and unconditional acceptance as the highest goods, and a group should grant what that account gets right, that shame-based criticism is genuinely destructive and that many people carry wounds that make them need to be received before they can be challenged. That is real, and the sequence matters, love first, then the hard word from inside the love. But the therapeutic account, taken alone, has no category for the faithful wound, and tends to read every hard truth as a violation of the self, which leaves a person surrounded by affirmation and unprotected from their own blind spots. Set this against the older wisdom of Proverbs, which assumes that a person cannot see themselves clearly and needs the loving correction of another to become who they should be, an anthropology that takes human self-deception seriously in a way the affirmation culture does not. Then take the harder turn toward the practice the church has nearly lost, the mutual accountability of Christian friendship, where believers were once expected to watch over one another's souls, to ask hard questions, to confess sin to one another and be restored. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, writing on Christian community in Life Together, argued that the person who is alone with their sin is utterly alone, and that the gift of a brother or sister is to break that isolation by hearing the truth and speaking it, so that confession and honest accountability are not intrusions on friendship but among its deepest offices. A group should ask honestly whether they have any friendship with that kind of permission in it, and whether the loss of such friendships has left a generation both more affirmed and more alone, praised constantly and known by no one. The aim is to recover honesty as an act of love, to refuse both the harshness that serves the speaker and the silence that abandons the friend, and to grant someone the terrifying, healing permission to tell us the truth.
sessions.caseStudy: A woman in your group is gentle and conflict-averse, the friend who never has a harsh word for anyone, proud that she is always encouraging and never critical. When the session names the faithful wound, she is genuinely troubled, because she has always believed her refusal to ever say a hard word was her best quality as a friend. Here is the gentle work for the leader, and it must honor her before it presses. Her gentleness is real and a genuine gift, and in a world full of critics the encouraging friend is precious, so do not treat her kindness as a fault. But notice what her conflict-avoidance may be costing the people she loves, because the friend who can never say a hard word is also the friend who watches you walk off a cliff and offers only encouragement on the way down. Her silence feels like kindness to her, but Proverbs would gently call it the hidden love that is worth less than open rebuke, and the people around her may be surrounded by her warmth and unprotected by her honesty. Do not shame her gentleness. Honor it fully, and still ask her, kindly, whether there is anyone she loves enough to risk their disapproval for their good, or whether her fear of conflict has quietly become a way of loving people without ever risking anything for them.

memoryVerse.text: Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy.

sessions.title: I Have Called You Friends
sessions.aim: To sit with the astonishing thing Jesus said the night before he died, that he no longer calls his followers servants but friends, and to see friendship not as a lesser love beneath the divine ones but as the very shape of the love God offers, refusing both the distant religion that keeps God a master and the sentimental one that makes him a buddy.
sessions.summary: Bell says the most staggering sentence about friendship in all of Scripture is not spoken by a poet or a king but by Jesus, on the last night of his life, to a room of men about to abandon him, and it is this, no longer do I call you servants, but I have called you friends. Stop at how strange that is, because everything about the relationship should run the other way. He is the Lord, they are the followers, the natural word is servant, and servant would have been generous. Instead, hours before the cross, he reaches past servant and says friend. The real question is what he means by it, because he defines it immediately and the definition is not sentimental. Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends, and then, this is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you. Friendship, in Jesus's mouth, is not the light and pleasant thing we have made it. It is the love that lays down its life. Bell takes the strong case for keeping God at a reverent distance, that calling God our friend is presumptuous and cheap, that it shrinks the Almighty into a buddy and loses the fear of the Lord. He grants the danger, and it is real, because a sentimental, chummy God who exists to affirm us is an idol, not the Holy One. But it was not we who reached up and claimed the friendship. It was God who reached down and named it, and he named it not from a safe distance but from inside the room where he was about to die for the friends who would run. Then the turn. Scripture had hinted at this all along, that God spoke to Moses face to face as a man speaks to his friend, that Abraham was called the friend of God, that Jesus was mocked as the friend of sinners and wore the insult as a title. The gospel is not mainly that God became our master. It is that the Holy One came near enough to call us friends, and then proved the word by dying for us.

keyScripture.why: No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing, but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you, Jesus reaching past the word servant to the word friend on the night before the cross, defining the relationship God offers not as distant mastery but as the intimacy of a friend who holds nothing back.

discussion.q: On the last night of his life, Jesus told a room of men who were about to abandon him that he no longer called them servants but friends. What is astonishing to you about that word, spoken at that moment, to those people?
discussion.behind: Open on the sheer strangeness before any doctrine. Everything about the relationship should make the word servant, and servant would already be gracious. That Jesus reaches past it to friend, hours before the cross, to men he knows will run, is almost scandalous. Help the room feel the weight of the word in its setting rather than skating over a phrase they have heard too often to hear.

discussion.q: Jesus defines friendship right after naming it, greater love has no one than to lay down his life for his friends. How does that definition compare to what you usually mean by the word friend?
discussion.behind: Press on the gap between his definition and ours. We use friend for the light, the pleasant, the casual. Jesus fills it with the heaviest love there is, self-sacrifice unto death. Help the room feel how far our usage has drifted from his, and let the size of his meaning expose how small ours has become, without scolding anyone for ordinary speech.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case that calling God our friend is presumptuous, that it shrinks the Almighty into a buddy and loses the fear of the Lord. What is true in that worry, and what would be lost if we let it silence the word Jesus actually used?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. The danger is real, a sentimental chummy God who exists to affirm us is an idol, and reverence matters. But the word was not our presumption, it was Jesus's gift, spoken by God himself. Help the room hold reverence and the offered friendship together, refusing both the cold distance that keeps God only a master and the cheap familiarity that makes him a mascot.

discussion.q: The friendship Jesus offers is not us reaching up to claim him but him reaching down to name us, from inside the room where he was about to die. How does it change things to know the friendship was God's initiative and not our presumption?
discussion.behind: Move to the heart of the gospel here. We did not earn or claim the friendship, and that is the relief. God named it first, at his own cost, toward people who would fail him. Help the room feel that this is grace, not achievement, and that the intimacy on offer is safe precisely because it rests on his initiative and his faithfulness rather than on our performance of it.

discussion.q: Jesus was mocked as the friend of sinners, and he wore the insult as a title. What does it mean for you that the friendship God offers is aimed precisely at the people the respectable would not befriend, and are you more comfortable being the friend or being befriended?
discussion.behind: Close on both the gift and the calling, and let it turn personal. Jesus befriended exactly the people friendship is usually rationed away from, and that is both the shape of grace toward us and the pattern for us. Help the room receive the astonishing thing, that they are befriended by God, and then feel the call, to befriend as he did, and go first by naming where you would rather keep friendship respectable and safe.

objections.objection: Calling God your friend is arrogant and casual. He is the Almighty, the maker of everything, and reducing him to a buddy you hang out with cheapens him and loses the reverence and fear that Scripture clearly commands.
objections.response: Grant the concern, because it is guarding something precious and Scripture guards it too. The fear of the Lord is real, God is holy and not tame, and a religion that has turned him into an affirming buddy who exists to boost our self-esteem has made an idol and lost the God of the burning bush and the whirlwind. That danger is not imaginary and should be named. Where the objection goes wrong is in aiming the charge of presumption at the wrong party, because it was not we who reached up and claimed the friendship. It was Jesus who reached down and named it, on the night before he died, and a word God himself chooses to describe his relationship with us is not ours to reject as too familiar. The wonder of the gospel is precisely that the Holy One, without ceasing to be holy, came near enough to call us friends, and the right response is not to correct him toward more distance but to be undone that the God we should fear has offered the intimacy we did not dare ask for. Reverence and friendship are not enemies here. The friend who died for us is the same Lord before whom we fall down.

objections.objection: If God is my friend, why does he feel so absent so often? Real friends show up, they answer when you call, they are present. A friend you cannot see or hear and who lets you suffer does not match anything I mean by friendship.
objections.response: Take the ache seriously, because it is honest and it is old, and the silence of God in suffering is one of the hardest things any believer carries, and no glib answer honors it. Grant the full weight of it. But hear what kind of friendship Jesus actually named, because he did not promise a friend who spares you all pain, he defined friendship as the one who lays down his life for his friends, and he defined it that way hours before he proved it on a cross. The friendship God offers is not the absence of suffering but his presence within it, which is a harder and deeper thing than the buddy who keeps trouble away. And the felt absence is not the whole story, because Scripture insists the friend who seems silent is the one who went into the grave ahead of us and promised never to leave. Jonathan crossed into David's wilderness. God crossed into ours, into death itself. That does not make the silence painless, and this study will not pretend it does. But it means the absence you feel is not abandonment. It is the presence of a friend who suffers with you in a way you cannot yet see, and who has already proved the friendship at the one place it counted most.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If Jesus said to you what he said to that room, that he no longer calls you a servant but a friend, would you be able to receive it, or would something in you insist on keeping him at the distance of a master?
sessions.practice: This week, sit with the sentence as if it were spoken to you, I have called you friends, and notice what rises, whether relief or resistance or the reflex to keep God at arm's length, and bring that honestly to him in prayer. And then do one thing that images his friendship outward, by befriending someone the way he befriended sinners, someone outside your comfortable circle, someone with nothing to offer you, someone the respectable would overlook. Write down what it stirs to be called a friend by God, and where you would rather keep both his friendship and your own too safe and too respectable to cost you anything.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, on the last night of your life, in a room full of men about to abandon you, you reached past the word servant, which would have been mercy enough, and you called them friends, and then you went out and proved the word by dying for them. We have made the word small, casual, cheap, and we have made you either a distant master we fear from far off or a buddy we no longer revere, and both are ways of refusing the friendship you actually offered. Forgive us. Teach us to receive the astonishing thing, that the Holy One came near enough to call us friends and then laid down his life to make it true. And teach us to befriend as you did, the sinner, the overlooked, the one with nothing to give, wearing the insult friend of sinners as the honor it always was. We are befriended by God. Make us worthy of the word by loving as you loved. Amen.
reflection: Can I actually receive being called a friend by God, or do I keep him at the safer distance of a master I serve but am not known by?
How far has my everyday use of the word friend drifted from the meaning Jesus filled it with, the love that lays down its life?
Where would I rather keep friendship respectable and safe, and how does the friend of sinners rebuke and reshape that instinct in me?
sessions.teaching: Bell says the single most staggering sentence about friendship in all of Scripture is not found in the Proverbs or in the story of David and Jonathan, and it is not spoken by a poet or a philosopher. It is spoken by Jesus, on the last night of his life, in an upper room, to a group of men he knows are hours from abandoning him, and it is this. No longer do I call you servants, but I have called you friends. To feel the force of it you have to refuse to let familiarity flatten it, because this is a sentence we have heard so often we have stopped hearing it at all. Consider who is speaking and to whom. He is the Lord, the one they have rightly called Teacher and Master, the one through whom, John has already told us, all things were made. They are his followers, his students, his servants, and servant is the honest word for the relationship, and servant would have been astonishingly generous coming from the mouth of God. A servant of the Most High is a title kings would envy. But Jesus does not stop at servant. Hours before he is arrested, hours before the cross, he reaches past the word that would already have been a gift, and he says friend. And then, because he knows we will sentimentalize it, he immediately defines it, and the definition has nothing soft in it. Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. And then, in the same breath, this is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you. So we have to reckon with what friendship means in the mouth of Jesus, because it is not the light and pleasant and optional thing we have made it. It is the heaviest love there is. It is the love that lays down its life. When he calls those men friends, he is not describing a pleasant association. He is telling them, on the eve of proving it, that friendship is the word for a love willing to die, and that he is about to die that death for the very friends who will run from the garden and deny him by a fire. Take the strong case for keeping God at a reverent distance, because it is serious and I feel its pull. Calling God your friend, the objection runs, is presumptuous and cheap. He is the Almighty, holy, other, the God of the burning bush who told Moses to take off his shoes, and to call him buddy is to shrink him to our size, to lose the fear of the Lord that Scripture commands, to trade the God of the whirlwind for a mascot who exists to affirm us. Grant the danger, all of it, because it is real and much of the modern church has fallen straight into it, manufacturing a chummy, sentimental, harmless God who is really just our own preferences with a halo. That God is an idol, and the reverence the objection is protecting is precious and right. But here is what the objection gets exactly wrong. It aims the charge of presumption at us, as if we were the ones who reached up and grabbed at a familiarity we had no right to. We did not. Read the sentence again and notice the direction of it. It was not the servants who announced they were now friends of the Master. It was the Master who reached down, from inside the room where he was about to die, and named the servants his friends. The friendship is not our presumption. It is his gift, and a word God himself chooses to describe how he relates to us is not ours to hand back as too intimate. And once you see that, the hints scattered across the whole of Scripture light up, because this was always where it was going. God spoke to Moses face to face, Exodus says, as a man speaks to his friend. Abraham was called, in three different books, the friend of God. And Jesus, in his own ministry, was sneered at by the respectable as a friend of tax collectors and sinners, and he did not deny the charge or soften it. He wore it. He let the insult stand as a title, because it was true, because befriending exactly the people friendship is usually rationed away from is the whole point of the kind of friend he is. Here is where it turns for me, and where I have to admit my own resistance. Raised without a father, come to faith out of atheism, I am far more comfortable with God as a master I serve than as a friend who knows me, because a master keeps his distance and a friend comes close, and closeness is the thing the self-protected heart has trained itself to avoid. I can serve God from across the room. Being called his friend asks me to let him near, and something in me would rather keep him at the reverent distance where I am safe. But the gospel will not leave me there. The gospel is not mainly that God became my master, though he is my Lord. It is that the Holy One, without laying down one ounce of his holiness, came near enough to call me friend, and then walked out of that upper room and proved the word at the one place words are proved, laying down his life for the friends who ran. That is the friendship on offer. Not a buddy who spares me trouble. A friend who went into the grave ahead of me and calls me, still, by the name I did not dare claim and could never have earned.

scriptureStudy.note: Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. Jesus defines friendship by the cross before he reaches it, filling the word with the heaviest love there is, and exposing how far our casual use of friend has drifted from what he meant by it.

You are my friends if you do what I command you. I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you. Friendship with Christ is marked by obedience and by disclosure, a master who hides nothing from those he now calls friends rather than servants.

This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you. The friendship Jesus offers is also a friendship he commands us to extend, the love received becoming the love we owe, measured by the impossible standard of the way he has loved us.

The Lord used to speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. Long before the upper room, Scripture dared to describe God's dealings with a man in the language of friendship, a face to face intimacy that anticipates what Jesus makes explicit.

Abraham believed God, and he was called a friend of God. The title friend of God is given to Abraham, showing that the friendship Jesus names was woven through the story from the beginning, offered by God and received by faith, not seized by human presumption.
